```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

`inferMM` targets a common enzyme-kinetic workflow: fit a Michaelis-Menten
curve, compare plausible working variance functions, and summarize inference in
a way that is less sensitive to heteroscedasticity than ordinary nonlinear least
squares alone. The same interface also supports clustered assay layouts in
which repeated measurements within a core, plate, or sample may be correlated.

## Single-curve fitting

```{r}
library(inferMM)

one_curve <- subset(sdl_demo, enzyme == "1111")

fit <- fit_mm(
  x = one_curve$s_uM,
  y = one_curve$v_uM_per_min,
  variance = "sqrt"
)

summary(fit)

fit_auto <- fit_mm(
  x = one_curve$s_uM,
  y = one_curve$v_uM_per_min,
  variance = "auto",
  power_selection = "quasi_aic"
)

summary(fit_auto)
```

The fitted object supports extraction of coefficients, Wald confidence
intervals, bootstrap confidence intervals, and predictions.

```{r}
coef(fit)
confint(fit)
set.seed(1)
confint(fit, method = "bootstrap", B = 99)
head(predict(fit, newdata = seq(0, 80, length.out = 6), interval = "prediction"))
```

For a one-step console summary plus a 95\% confidence band, use:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
report_mm(fit, interval_type = "confidence")
set.seed(1)
report_mm(fit, method = "bootstrap", B = 99,
          interval_type = "confidence")
```

## Screening working variance models

```{r}
screen <- screen_mm(
  x = one_curve$s_uM,
  y = one_curve$v_uM_per_min,
  power_values = c(0.4, 0.6),
  include_auto = TRUE,
  quiet = TRUE
)

screen$table[, c("model", "selected_model", "quasi_aic", "quasi_bic", "rmse")]
```

The screening table is ordered by quasi-AIC, with quasi-BIC and RMSE reported
as secondary summaries.

## User-defined fixed variance functions

For a single curve, a function can replace a built-in variance name. It defines
the shape `h(S)` in `Var(Y | S) = gamma h(S)`, not the standard deviation.

```{r}
h <- variance_function(function(S) 1 + S / 20,
                       label = "Var = gamma (1 + S/20)")
custom_fit <- fit_mm(one_curve$s_uM, one_curve$v_uM_per_min, variance = h)
summary(custom_fit)
confint(custom_fit)
predict(custom_fit, newdata = c(0, 10, 40), interval = "prediction")

custom_shapes <- list(
  linear_floor = function(S) 1 + S / 20,
  saturation = function(S) 1 + 9 * S / (20 + S)
)
custom_screen <- screen_mm(
  one_curve$s_uM, one_curve$v_uM_per_min,
  variance_models = c("constant", "sqrt"),
  variance_functions = custom_shapes, quiet = TRUE
)
custom_screen$table[, c("model", "quasi_aic", "quasi_bic", "success")]
```

The function must be deterministic, vectorized, and pointwise, returning one
finite strictly positive numeric value for each input concentration, including
zero if used. Values must not depend on the other concentrations in the vector.
For example, a constant shape should return `rep(1, length(S))`, not a scalar.
Invalid values or lengths cause errors; screening records candidate-specific
errors and continues with the remaining candidates. Names must be unique and
must not duplicate built-in candidates. For custom-only screening, specify
`variance_models = character(0)`.

Only Km requires numerical search for a fixed shape. Vmax and gamma retain their
closed-form updates, and the function is reused for prediction and bootstrap
refits. Internal scaling preserves the supplied variance model. The reported
gamma is relative to the original shape, so its value changes inversely when
the shape is multiplied by a positive constant.

The constants 20 and 9 above are fixed, not estimated. Extra shape parameters,
functions of unknown mean parameters, and data-adaptive nuisance estimation are
not fitted by this interface. Intervals and information criteria condition on
the supplied shape and omit external shape-estimation or selection uncertainty;
prediction bands still use the working-normal approximation. User-defined
variance shapes are not higher-moment efficient scores and do not imply smaller
variance than identically weighted WNLS. They are currently supported for
independent curves, not the clustered routine.

## Optional higher-moment estimation for independent curves

The user-defined variance shape above does not by itself incorporate
asymmetry into the estimating equations. Version 0.1.1 adds the separate
`fit_mm_moments()` estimator, based on the conditional-moment construction
of Kim and Ma (2012), Section 3 (doi:10.1007/s10463-011-0332-y).
It does not require a fully specified error density.

```{r}
set.seed(19)
skew_dat <- simulate_mm_data(n = 200, error = "skewed", skew_shape = 4)
assay_shape <- function(S) 1 + 9 * S / (20 + S)
fit_hm <- fit_mm_moments(skew_dat$x, skew_dat$y, variance = assay_shape)
summary(fit_hm)
confint(fit_hm)
fit_hm$vcov_joint

fit_gamma <- fit_mm_moments(
  skew_dat$x, skew_dat$y, variance = assay_shape,
  moments = "gamma", shape = 4
)
coef(fit_gamma)
predict(fit_gamma, c(10, 20, 80), interval = "confidence")
```

The default estimates constant standardized skewness and kurtosis from the
profile pilot's residuals. The gamma option supplies fixed working moments
of **centered** gamma errors; it does not fit a gamma density. Student-t
working moments use `moments = "student_t", df = 10`. Custom standardized
moment functions can be passed with `moments = "custom"`, `skewness`, and
`kurtosis`; the latter is raw kurtosis, not excess kurtosis.

For residual $r_i$ and variance $v_i=\gamma h(S_i)$, let
$u_i=(r_i,r_i^2-v_i)^\top$. The conditional moment covariance is

$$
\Omega_i=\begin{pmatrix}
v_i & s_i v_i^{3/2}\\
s_i v_i^{3/2} & (k_i-1)v_i^2
\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $s_i$ and $k_i$ are working skewness and kurtosis. With $g_i$ the MM
mean gradient and
$D_i=\begin{pmatrix}g_{i1}&g_{i2}&0\\0&0&h(S_i)\end{pmatrix}$,
the joint equation is $\sum_i D_i^\top\Omega_i^{-1}u_i=0$.
Positive definiteness requires $k_i-1-s_i^2>0$.

Unlike the default profile route, the higher-moment fit solves jointly for
$V_{\max},K_m,\gamma$ numerically. Its default `covariance = "model"`
uses joint inverse working information, with the mean covariance extracted
after allowing for the estimated scale. This interpretation requires
appropriate conditional third and fourth moments. Optional
`covariance = "sandwich"` uses the complete three-parameter equations.
Wald intervals use a normal cutoff
for the estimator, not an assumption that the individual errors are normal.

Normal moments recover the original mean/variance equations. Constant
symmetric Student-t moments recover the same point estimates; heavy tails
alone do not give an efficiency improvement in this conditional-moment
model. Under asymmetry, appropriate third/fourth moments can improve
asymptotic efficiency, but pilot moment estimation can inflate finite-sample
variance. Incorrect variance shapes can bias the new estimator, and a
sandwich does not remove that bias. Neither exact 95% coverage nor uniform
improvement is guaranteed.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(20)
confint(fit_hm, method = "bootstrap", B = 399)  # pairs only
report_mm(fit_hm, interval_type = "confidence")
```

Pairs bootstrap repeats the pilot and higher-moment estimation. Prediction
bands are not supplied because a few moments do not identify predictive
quantiles; mean-confidence bands are pointwise. Quasi-AIC/BIC are omitted
for these non-likelihood roots. This opt-in estimator is not yet connected
to grouped selection or clustered fitting; those workflows below retain
their original estimators.

## Grouped analyses

For real enzyme panels we often fit many curves at once and then compare the
best model within each group.

```{r}
grouped <- group_mm(
  data = sdl_demo,
  s = "s_uM",
  v = "v_uM_per_min",
  groups = "enzyme",
  variance_models = c("constant", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"),
  power_values = c(0.4, 0.6),
  include_auto = TRUE,
  variance_functions = custom_shapes,
  quiet = TRUE
)

head(grouped$comparison$best_by_group[, c("group_label", "model", "selected_model", "quasi_aic", "quasi_bic", "rmse")])
```

To visualize the current best model for each group, use the grouped plotting
method.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plot(grouped, interval_type = "confidence")
```

## Clustered repeated measurements

By default, `cluster_mm()` uses a rank-one working covariance with a random
effect on `Vmax` and a low-dimensional
residual variance function. The bundled `alves_demo` data illustrate the
interface on a small soil-enzyme panel.

```{r}
cluster_fit <- cluster_mm(
  data = subset(alves_demo, enzyme == "BG"),
  s = "substrate_conc",
  v = "activity",
  cluster = "core",
  variance = "sqrt"
)

summary(cluster_fit)
confint(cluster_fit)
head(predict(cluster_fit, newdata = seq(0, 700, length.out = 6),
             interval = "confidence"))
```

Because the bundled example contains only three cores, the printed summary
reports point estimates by default and treats interval output as an explicit
sensitivity analysis.

An optional `method = "projected"` uses an MM-specific adaptation of
Ma and Genton (2010, Section 3.2),
<https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2010.00741.x>. It leaves the random-effect
density unspecified while retaining conditionally independent Gaussian
residuals with a correct fixed variance shape. The identity-instrument
projected score does not generally attain the semiparametric efficiency bound.
Standard errors use a stacked independent-cluster sandwich, and only
mean-confidence bands are returned. At least five clusters and two readings
per cluster are required; this path is therefore not applied to the three-core
example above. The package README provides a reproducible skewed-random-effect
example. This is distinct from non-Gaussian independent residual estimation.

Projected failures report a numerical stage, reason and available diagnostics
in `inferMM_cluster_projected_error`; no estimate or interval is returned and
no automatic method switch occurs. An incomplete numerical search can retain
a verified interior root but warns explicitly. Inspect `fit$convergence`,
especially the scaled joint score norm and search diagnostics. A non-positive
variance-component moment has a separate reporting warning. For the default
profile method, an iteration-limit warning marks `converged = FALSE`; such
results should not be interpreted as converged fits.

## Simulation

```{r}
set.seed(100)
sim_dat <- simulate_mm_data(variance_shape = "hill", error = "skewed")
head(sim_dat)
```

The package is intentionally lightweight: it relies only on base and
recommended R packages, while keeping the workflow close to the heteroscedastic
and clustered Michaelis-Menten analyses used in the companion methodology
paper.
